descriptions.value: The 1975-1990 Lebanese Civil War was a 15-year sectarian conflict that officially ran from April 13, 1975 to October 13, 1990, triggered by an attack on a Christian church in Beirut that escalated into large-scale armed clashes between Christian-aligned and Muslim-aligned sectarian militias. The core underlying cause of the conflict was disagreement over the presence and operations of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) in Lebanese territory, with Lebanese Muslim factions supporting the PLO's use of Lebanon as a base for attacks against Israel, while Christian factions opposed the PLO's presence. The conflict quickly led to the division of Beirut into sectarian enclaves separated by the 'Green Line' boundary between Christian-held East Beirut and Muslim/PLO-held West Beirut, and the formal collapse of the Lebanese coalition government by September 1975, accompanied by an estimated 8 billion pounds in property damage and widespread capital flight from the country.

descriptions.value: The war formally ended on October 13, 1990, following the negotiation and implementation of the Taif Agreement, which reformed Lebanon's confessional power-sharing framework by adjusting Christian-to-Muslim parliamentary representation from a 55:45 ratio to 50:50, and strengthened the political powers of the Muslim-reserved Prime Minister post relative to the Christian-reserved President post. Key long-term outcomes of the conflict included Syrian occupation of northern and eastern Lebanon until April 2005, Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon until May 2000, the formation and rise of the Iranian-backed Shiite militia Hezbollah as a dominant political and military force in Lebanon, and the disarmament of all other Lebanese and non-Lebanese militias operating in the country.
